title: Implementing feedback in creative systems: a workshop approach
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how feedback can be incorporated into computational creativity systems, with a broader interest in how AI systems can learn from interaction and critique. The authors argue that feedback is fundamental to creativity and learning, but that computational creativity systems have largely not treated feedback as a central design feature.

To tackle this, the paper proposes the Writers Workshop as a computational model for structured critique. In the proposed workflow, an author/system presents work, critics listen and provide feedback, the author asks clarifying questions, critics respond, and the author reflects and potentially updates its internal model or codebase. The paper develops this as a conceptual framework and illustrates it with a dialogue example and a case study in the FloWr flowchart-based creative system, focusing on computer poetry.

The intended context is not K-12 education but AI and computational creativity research. The paper suggests that a workshop-style protocol could support serendipity, constructive critique, and mutual learning among autonomous systems, and it briefly notes that similar ideas might someday be relevant for educational feedback. Its main conclusion is that a structured workshop model is a promising roadmap for feedback-driven AI systems, though the paper is primarily theoretical and implementation-oriented rather than an empirical evaluation of effectiveness.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper proposing a writers-workshop-inspired feedback model for computational creativity systems. It does not evaluate a K-12 educational intervention, does not report an empirical study with student or teacher outcomes, and provides only illustrative examples and a preliminary implementation discussion.
impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured impact on learners, teachers, or schools. The paper’s relevance to K-12 teacher-facing generative AI coaching is indirect and speculative, so no educational effect size or practical impact can be inferred.
